title: The One Where Chandler Gets Caught

jokes.text: My God, get a room. / I would get a room with this cake. / I think I could show this cake a good time.
jokes.setup: Someone exclaims 'get a room' as an expression of exasperation at another person's enthusiasm for cake
jokes.punchline: The characters escalate by literally entertaining the idea of a romantic relationship with the cake, culminating in 'I could show this cake a good time'
jokes.explanation: A solid cold-open escalation joke. The pivot from idiom to literal meaning is well-timed, and 'show this cake a good time' is a funny line. Not especially character-specific but efficiently built.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this cake is amazing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Get a room.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're in a room. And if this cake were here, I'd never leave it.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm sorry, honey. But when she said 'sex,' I wasn't thinking about sex with you.
jokes.setup: The group asks who would give up food vs. sex, and Ross's girlfriend/wife answers 'sex' instantly — implying she'd give it up for food
jokes.punchline: Ross admits he answered 'sex' quickly too — but clarifies he wasn't thinking of sex WITH her, implying he was mentally picturing someone else
jokes.explanation: A deceptively sharp joke. The setup (embarrassed apology) makes you expect him to walk it back; the punchline makes it far worse. The structure is tight, the reveal lands as a double cringe — he's both a bad partner AND accidentally honest. Strong audience impact.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Sex or food?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Sex.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was fast!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What did you expect? I'm gonna think about meatloaf?

jokes.text: It's like a giant hug. [said about the cake]
jokes.setup: The group has been treating cake with romantic/sexual language
jokes.punchline: Monica's sincere, tender description of cake as 'a giant hug' is funnier precisely because it's NOT sexual — it's weirdly wholesome and deeply Monica
jokes.explanation: Best asset is character integration — this is exactly the kind of earnest, food-obsessed sincerity that defines Monica. Short and punchy. Not a huge laugh but a genuine character moment that gets a smile.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to sound so quick about that.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, what were you thinking about?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Janice.

jokes.text: Ross, how about you? Which would you give up? Food. / How about sex or dinosaurs?
jokes.setup: Ross quickly answers 'food' in the food-vs-sex question
jokes.punchline: The follow-up question 'Sex or dinosaurs?' reframes Ross's priorities — implying dinosaurs would be a harder choice for him than sex
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific joke. The genius is that it needs no punchline tag — the question itself IS the punchline because everyone in the room (and audience) knows Ross's obsession. Tight economy, high character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Food is like a giant hug for your stomach.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's the saddest thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, it's like Sophie's Choice.
jokes.setup: Ross is asked whether he'd give up sex or dinosaurs
jokes.punchline: He invokes Sophie's Choice — a film about an impossibly tragic life-or-death moral dilemma — to describe the difficulty of choosing between sex and dinosaurs
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of a Holocaust drama reference with the trivial dilemma is well-calibrated. It works because Ross plays it completely sincerely. A good cultural-reference joke that earns rather than coasts.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, Ross, I'm gonna give you an even harder choice: it's a toss-up between a woman and a dinosaur.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wha— that's not even a choice!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, come on. A woman or a dinosaur? You're telling me you wouldn't even have to think about that?

jokes.text: Food. No, sex. Food. Sex. Food. Sex-- I don't know! Oh, God, I want both!
jokes.setup: Joey is asked the food-or-sex question
jokes.punchline: His anguished back-and-forth followed by 'I want both!' — building to an absurd climax that perfectly captures Joey's id-driven character
jokes.explanation: Joey's whole persona is appetite — both literal and romantic. The escalating indecision is very well-performed and character-driven. The rhythm of repetition before the breakdown is structurally sound.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, that's like asking me to choose between sex and dinosaurs. I mean, they're both things I love.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like that movie Schindler's List — it's a great film, but I'm not gonna watch it every night.

jokes.text: I want-- I want girls on bread!
jokes.setup: Joey has been agonizing over choosing between food and sex
jokes.punchline: His solution: combine them — 'girls on bread' — a gloriously absurd non-sequitur that is both stupid and perfectly Joey
jokes.explanation: The best joke of the cold open and one of the episode's strongest. 'Girls on bread' is a brilliant piece of comedic economy — three words that are simultaneously absurd, logical within Joey's food-sex framework, and completely character-specific. It has the quality of a great Joey line: childlike, sincere, and deeply weird. High quotability, big audience reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Food or sex? Food or sex? Food... sex... food... sex...

jokes.text: Oh, no, that is a doll. / Oh, thank God, because that thing's really creepy.
jokes.setup: Someone says 'She looks just like a little doll' about a photo of Emma
jokes.punchline: Rachel clarifies it literally IS a doll — then Phoebe expresses relief because she found the image creepy
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection setup and payoff — the metaphor becomes literal. Phoebe's relief adds a nice tag that gently insults Rachel's baby. Efficient and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why choose? I'm gonna have sex on a pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, that's disgusting.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? It's still warm!

jokes.text: He's having an affair. / He is not having an affair! / I'm always right about these things. / No, you're not. Last week, you thought Ross was trying to kill you.
jokes.setup: Phoebe immediately declares Chandler is having an affair upon seeing him with a blonde woman
jokes.punchline: Rachel counters that Phoebe is not 'always right' — citing last week when Phoebe thought Ross was trying to kill her
jokes.explanation: The punchline about Phoebe thinking Ross was trying to kill her is perfectly Phoebe — paranoid, oblivious, and sincere. Good character specificity. The escalation from 'affair' to 'murder conspiracy' is nicely absurd.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look how cute Emma looks in this photo!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, right? She's adorable.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait... is this a doll?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's a doll.

jokes.text: Well, sorry, but it's hard to believe that anyone would tell a story that dull just to tell it.
jokes.setup: Rachel pushes back on Phoebe's murder theory about Ross
jokes.punchline: Phoebe defends herself by suggesting Ross's dull story must have had a sinister ulterior motive — because why else would anyone tell it?
jokes.explanation: Funny because it's both a character moment (Phoebe's wild leaps of logic) and a casual burn on Ross's storytelling. The implication that his stories are so dull they must be cover for murder is a great character cross-reference.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh thank God, it's just a doll.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I was so worried Emma actually looked like that.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, that would be... not good.

jokes.text: Okay, duck down. [Phoebe and Rachel literally duck down in a cab to tail Chandler]
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Rachel have decided to follow Chandler's cab like detectives
jokes.punchline: The visual of two adult women dramatically ducking down in a cab to avoid being spotted by their friend — spy-movie behavior applied to mundane friend drama
jokes.explanation: Functional visual comedy derived from the absurdity of the situation. The humor is in the commitment to the bit rather than any specific line.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, no. He's trying to kill me! He tells these boring stories just to make me fall asleep so he can smother me with a pillow.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Is it? Is it really? Because he's been telling a lot of really boring stories lately.

jokes.text: Oh, I have to work too. Yeah, I'm stuck here at the office all day.
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls to invite Chandler to the movies, checking if he's free
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Chandler is literally not at the office — he's out with a realtor. The audience watches him lie in real time, with Phoebe and Rachel secretly watching him
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony played for comedy — the audience is in on the lie, Phoebe and Rachel are watching him lie. Situational rather than line-driven.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: How about 'Sleeping with the Enemy'?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Or 'Betrayal'?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: 'Liar Liar'?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Phoebe, I'm not cheating on Monica!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Then why won't you come home?

jokes.text: Because we were gonna see Liar Liar... or Betrayal or An Affair to Remember.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to guilt or bait Chandler about his suspected affair via movie titles
jokes.punchline: The movie titles are all thematically loaded — Liar Liar, Betrayal, An Affair to Remember — delivered innocently as if just listing films
jokes.explanation: A clever sustained gag — Phoebe weaponizes movie titles as passive-aggressive hints. The escalation from one to three titles, each more on-the-nose, is well-constructed. Character-appropriate because Phoebe does things sideways.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: These movies are like fifty years old.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! What about... Ghostbusters?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, why would we watch Ghostbusters?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because there's a ghost in our apartment!

jokes.text: Those are all really old. / Okay, then maybe it'll be-- / Dude, Where's My Car? / What? / They're in a car.
jokes.setup: Chandler dismisses Phoebe's suspiciously loaded movie suggestions as 'really old,' so Rachel needs a newer title that also fits
jokes.punchline: Rachel blurts 'Dude, Where's My Car?' — a terrible thematic fit — then justifies it with the pathetically literal 'They're in a car'
jokes.explanation: The pivot to a completely non-applicable movie and then Rachel's weak justification is well-executed. The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of the choice and Rachel's desperate post-hoc rationalization. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, Phoebe. Why don't you just follow him in a cab? I'm sure that won't be weird at all.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know! I'll need spy gear.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Spy gear? Phoebe, I was being sarcastic.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I know. I have binoculars, a fake mustache, and a camera disguised as a shoe.

jokes.text: Yeah, okay. Let me just grab my night-vision goggles and my stun gun. / I got them.
jokes.setup: Rachel sarcastically agrees to follow Chandler's cab, listing spy gear she obviously doesn't have
jokes.punchline: Phoebe matter-of-factly confirms she actually HAS the night-vision goggles and stun gun
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup-punchline with a perfect character-specific kicker. Rachel's sarcasm is assumed to be normal hyperbole; Phoebe's sincere 'I got them' instantly upends expectations and deepens the joke with Phoebe's lovably eccentric character. The economy is superb — two words do all the work. Among the episode's sharpest jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And this room has excellent... um... feng shui flow and natural luminosity with a hint of architectural... je ne sais quoi!

jokes.text: Hey, you smell like perfume and cigarettes. / Nancy doesn't smoke. / Well, at least the perfume's not mine. Be thankful for that.
jokes.setup: Monica notices Chandler smells like another woman's perfume and cigarettes — potential affair clues
jokes.punchline: Chandler deflects with 'at least the perfume's not mine' — a weird flex that is somehow both reassuring and suspicious
jokes.explanation: Decent deflection joke. The logic of 'at least it's not my perfume' is delightfully absurd as a form of reassurance. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more worked up about this house?

jokes.text: And the wiggle woms and the zip zorps!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Nancy are describing house features to Monica — wainscoting, crown molding, dormer windows
jokes.punchline: Chandler, clearly not knowing the real terminology, invents completely made-up architectural words: 'wiggle woms' and 'zip zorps'
jokes.explanation: Funny because Chandler is clearly out of his depth in the real estate conversation and is essentially freestyling. 'Wiggle woms' and 'zip zorps' are inspired nonsense words — the sounds are inherently funny. Good character moment and highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How badly do you want to smoke?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm seeing you as a cigarette right now.

jokes.text: This is bringing out a lovely color in you.
jokes.setup: Monica is clearly excited and flushed about the house, possibly visibly emotional or energized
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry comment that the excitement is 'bringing out a lovely color' in her — an absurd, slightly romantic compliment for a weird moment
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deadpan. It's a sweet-funny line that shows his affection for Monica while still being a good dry joke. Character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So, um, about that cab ride to Westchester... does anyone want to chip in?

jokes.text: I don't know what you mean, giant, talking cigarette.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Monica how much she wants to smoke, knowing she quit
jokes.punchline: Monica deflects in total denial, addressing Chandler as 'giant, talking cigarette' — she's so deep in withdrawal she's hallucinating
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The absurdist image of Monica seeing Chandler as 'a giant, talking cigarette' in her nicotine-withdrawal haze is inventive and perfectly economical. The line does triple duty: it's a denial joke, an absurdist image joke, and a character moment. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Would you want to know if Mike was cheating on you?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? No! Why would you say that? Is Mike cheating on me? Did he tell you something?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, no, it's just a hypothetical.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God. It's not hypothetical! You know something! What do you know?

jokes.text: Oh, my God, that is gonna be so hard. / I know. Good luck with it.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Monica to keep the house secret; she immediately agrees
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually says 'good luck with it' to Monica — the person famously incapable of keeping secrets — which is a mild self-aware acknowledgment of her character flaw
jokes.explanation: A quiet character-comedy moment. The joke is in knowing Monica's history with secrets — a wink to long-term viewers. Not explosive but earns its laugh through accumulated character knowledge.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I wish I had a smaller sponge.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: There are so many places I can't reach with this one.

jokes.text: Chandler? Forty-five minutes? [group reacts to 45-minute timeframe with disappointed implications about Chandler's stamina]
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells the group that Chandler and the blonde were in the house together for 45 minutes
jokes.punchline: The characters' pause on '45 minutes' implies it's either too short or meaningfully long for an affair — played as a knowing reaction beat
jokes.explanation: Decent reaction beat. The implied joke about Chandler's sexual stamina (or timing) lands as a mild audience chuckle. Gets paid off later with a bigger version of this joke.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: An affair? In this neighborhood?

jokes.text: If one of us saw Mike with another woman, would you want us to tell you? / Why? Who'd you see him with? / No one! I'm just saying if we did-- / Tell me what you know!
jokes.setup: Rachel poses a hypothetical about whether Phoebe would want to know if Mike were cheating
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately treats it as a confession rather than a hypothetical, escalating to 'Tell me what you know!' with increasing desperation
jokes.explanation: Nicely escalating exchange that rings very true to Phoebe's character — she short-circuits the hypothetical framework immediately. 'Tell me what you know!' is a funny, paranoid demand. Good structure and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Son of a bitch!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, hello to you too.

jokes.text: If I did see him with someone, there's no way I-- / Who did you see him with?
jokes.setup: Rachel has just convinced Phoebe that it was hypothetical and Mike is faithful
jokes.punchline: Rachel begins a new hypothetical sentence and Phoebe instantly pounces again — 'Who did you see him with?' — unable to let it go
jokes.explanation: A callback that works because it shows Phoebe hasn't moved on at all despite being reassured. The repetition structure amplifies the joke rather than repeating it flatly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, so you weren't having an affair?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No! Of course not!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. For a second there I thought... well, I mean, who would even... I mean, come on, it's you.

jokes.text: If only there were a smaller one to clean this one.
jokes.setup: Monica is cleaning something, clearly content with domestic tasks
jokes.punchline: Monica wishes for a smaller version of whatever she's cleaning, so she could clean the cleaner — an ouroboros of cleanliness obsession
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Monica's compulsive cleaning psychology. The recursive logic (needing a tool to clean the tool) is both funny and deeply true to character. Strong character integration score.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler and I have decided to move out.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're getting our own place.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Guys, we need to talk about this as a group.

jokes.text: Look, whatever happens, we're here for you, and we love you. / All right. / Chandler might be having an affair.
jokes.setup: Phoebe delivers an ominous, over-solemn speech ('whatever happens, we're here for you') building enormous dread
jokes.punchline: After the dramatic pause, the 'big news' is delivered flatly by Rachel: 'Chandler might be having an affair' — the buildup vastly outweighs the revelation
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the structural mismatch — Phoebe's melodramatic preamble vs. the relatively matter-of-fact delivery of the news. Good construction.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I want a house with a big yard, and a swing set, and maybe an ice cream truck parked out front.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, that's not a house. That's a memory.

jokes.text: Did you think the neighborhood was homey?
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Rachel have just told Monica that Chandler is cheating; Monica appears devastated
jokes.punchline: Monica's response is to ask about the neighborhood of the house — revealing she already knows about the realtor, and her 'devastation' was performance
jokes.explanation: A great structural joke. Monica's question is perfectly incongruous with the emotional setup — it completely derails the dramatic scene and is the reveal that she knows. The economy of using one misplaced question to do all that work is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Leave New York? Are you crazy? This is the greatest city in the world!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where else can you get a pizza at 3 in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And the women! The women are everywhere, and they're all single and looking for a guy who's an actor.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Plus, there's this guy on my block who sells loose cigarettes out of his apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, what more could you want?

jokes.text: Hey. / You son of a bitch.
jokes.setup: Chandler walks in cheerfully saying 'Hey'
jokes.punchline: Monica's immediate flat 'You son of a bitch' — before he's even said anything — signals she's playing along with the ruse while Phoebe and Rachel are still present
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Chandler's breezy greeting and Monica's instant profanity is a timing joke that depends on the audience knowing more than Monica's friends. The punchline's brevity ('you son of a bitch') is its greatest asset — maximum impact in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You guys are moving out of the city?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But... but you can't leave me! I'm gonna die!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm serious! I can't live without you guys. I don't know how to cook, I don't know how to clean, and I barely know how to dress myself!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: If you move away, I swear I will... I will never, ever watch one of your movies again, Chandler!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Actually, I don't watch them anyway, but NOW it means something!

jokes.text: Is it me, or have the greetings gone downhill around here?
jokes.setup: Monica just called Chandler 'you son of a bitch' as a greeting
jokes.punchline: Chandler's breezy meta-observation about the declining quality of greetings in his apartment
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deflection humor — using sardonic meta-observation to process a hostile situation. Character-perfect and efficiently delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We already made an offer on a house.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? An affair would be better news right now.

jokes.text: I knew he couldn't be with a woman for 45 minutes!
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals Nancy is their realtor, not a mistress — explaining the innocent 45-minute house visit
jokes.punchline: Phoebe takes the revelation as vindication, but her reasoning is a backhand insult about Chandler's sexual stamina — 'he couldn't be with a woman for 45 minutes'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a perfect callback payoff. The genius is that Phoebe thinks she's defending Chandler while simultaneously insulting him. The structure is airtight: the '45 minutes' detail planted earlier pays off here with a double meaning. Character-perfect for Phoebe — obliviously devastating. Very high quotability and audience impact.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I love the streams and the maple trees.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know who else loves streams and maple trees? Beavers. You're basically a beaver.

jokes.text: What is wrong with raising a kid in the city? I'm doing it. Ross is doing it. Sarah Jessica Parker is doing it!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica defend wanting to raise their child outside the city
jokes.punchline: Rachel escalates her list of city-parent examples to include Sarah Jessica Parker — a celebrity name-drop that is both incongruously famous and vaguely relevant (she's a NYC icon)
jokes.explanation: The celebrity name-drop escalation is a familiar sitcom move. Gets a mild chuckle from the incongruity of Rachel citing SJP as peer-level evidence. Not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're moving? Both of you? But... but how am I supposed to stop eating all the food in the apartment if you guys aren't here to judge me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I mean, I've tried to stop before. I can't do it. I have no self-control. If the food is there, I will eat it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You're like my food conscience. Without you, I'm just gonna turn into a big fat... well, a bigger fat Joey.

jokes.text: So you want to buy a house in the '50s.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica describe the idyllic suburban life they want: lawn, swing set, kids riding bikes, ice cream truck
jokes.punchline: Ross's dry one-liner equates their vision with idealized 1950s Americana, implying it's nostalgic fantasy rather than modern reality
jokes.explanation: A compact, sharp line. Ross's academic/analytical tendency to contextualize everything historically is on-brand, and the observation is genuinely funny. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I was like, 'Oh my God, he's having an affair,' but then I was like, 'But look at this crown molding!'

jokes.text: What if you want Chinese food at 5 a.m.? Or a fake Rolex that breaks as soon as it rains? Or an Asian hooker sent right to your door?
jokes.setup: Joey tries to list reasons Chandler and Monica shouldn't leave the city
jokes.punchline: Joey's escalating list of 'city perks' degenerates from (arguably) reasonable (Chinese food at 5am) to absurd (fake Rolexes) to wildly inappropriate
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure works until the last item, which is cheap shock humor that hasn't aged well. The joke coasts on Joey's obliviousness as a character shield, but the final punchline relies on a stereotype rather than wit. Below average on earned_vs_cheap.

jokes.text: It's okay, because they have to get it out of their system. But you're gonna realize this is the only place you want to be.
jokes.setup: Joey and Ross are loudly protesting the move; Monica tries to calm things down
jokes.punchline: Chandler speaks ABOUT the friends AS IF they're not in the room, with amused condescension — 'they have to get it out of their system' — treating adults like tantrum-throwing children
jokes.explanation: Pleasant comic beat — Chandler's condescension toward his own friends is very on-brand. Functional but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you just said, but it sounds like you're upset.

jokes.text: Bet you wish I was having an affair now, huh?
jokes.setup: The friends have just found out Chandler and Monica put an offer on a house
jokes.punchline: Chandler's perfectly timed quip suggests the friends would have preferred adultery to this news — a great inversion of expected values
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The inversion — that an affair would have been BETTER news than moving to the suburbs — is sharp, economical, and perfectly delivered. It's a callback that lands as a whole-episode punchline. High marks across craft dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You know what? I just realized something. 'Coincidence' and 'join' sound kind of the same... So I'm going to start saying 'joincidence' instead.

jokes.text: Oh, again with the nature. What are you, beavers?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are describing their dream house (yard, stream, maple trees)
jokes.punchline: Ross's exasperated 'What are you, beavers?' — using an animal associated with trees and streams as a dismissive punchline
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-constructed animal comparison that works because beavers genuinely are associated with the nature imagery being described. Tight and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that Ugly Naked Guy with romantic candles?

jokes.text: Is this because I come over here without knocking and eat your food? Because I can stop doing that. I really, really think I can.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are explaining they're moving for the baby's sake — nothing to do with the friends
jokes.punchline: Joey interprets the move as punishment for his freeloading behavior — and his 'I really, really think I can' is an obviously unconvincing attempt at self-improvement
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey self-awareness moment. His attribution of blame to himself is funny on its own, but 'I really, really think I can' is the punchline — the qualifier 'really, really think' signals he absolutely cannot stop. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that Ugly Naked Guy with candles?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, looks romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Romantic? The guy's on fire!

jokes.text: I can't believe Chandler's screwing this woman, but man, this would be a nice place to live!
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Rachel to back him up on the house being beautiful — she was there
jokes.punchline: Rachel admits the house was gorgeous, then reveals her internal monologue was simultaneously indicting Chandler of adultery while admiring the real estate
jokes.explanation: A good callback that gets mileage from Rachel's ability to compartmentalize moral judgment and real estate appreciation simultaneously. The juxtaposition is well-structured and character-appropriate for shallow-but-lovable Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, you've reorganized my entire station three times in the last hour.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm just trying to make sure everything is perfect!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Perfect? Monica, you color-coded the spices. We're making turkey, not launching a space shuttle.

jokes.text: Come on, Daddy, listen! All my life, everyone's always told me 'You're a shoe!' 'You're a shoe! You're a shoe!' I stopped and said, 'What if I don't want to be a shoe? What if I want to be a purse? Or a hat?'
jokes.setup: Ross is resisting the idea that Chandler and Monica could change — the friends are arguing about moving
jokes.punchline: Rachel delivers an impassioned speech using her own backstory as metaphor — she was told she'd always be a 'shoe' (dependent socialite) but became her own person. The 'shoe' metaphor is unintentionally absurdist.
jokes.explanation: A self-referential Rachel character moment — her journey from sheltered rich girl to independent woman, filtered through fashion metaphor. The humor is in how earnest and slightly ridiculous the metaphor is ('you're a shoe'), which then gets punctured perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It smells bad in here!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's because you're stuck in a dead bird.

jokes.text: I don't want you to buy me a hat, I-- / It's a metaphor, Daddy!
jokes.setup: Rachel has just delivered her emotional 'shoe/purse/hat' metaphor speech
jokes.punchline: Ross takes it literally — thinking Rachel wants a hat — requiring Rachel to snap back 'It's a metaphor, Daddy!'
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. Ross's literalism (he actually thought she wanted a hat) is perfectly in-character, and 'It's a metaphor, Daddy!' has great rhythm and quotability. The 'Daddy' adds a weird, funny layer to the correction.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, how many categories of towels are there?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, there's bath towels, hand towels, washcloths, guest towels, fancy towels, everyday towels, and decorative towels.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica, those are just... towels. They all dry you off. That's it. That's the only category that matters.

jokes.text: You can see where he'd have trouble.
jokes.setup: Ross has just confused Rachel's metaphor for a request for a hat
jokes.punchline: Chandler's dry aside acknowledging that the metaphor WAS confusing — a mild defense of Ross that doubles as a critique of Rachel's speech
jokes.explanation: A quick, perfectly timed Chandler aside. Classic one-liner that gets its laugh from brevity and timing rather than complexity.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Transponster!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's not even a word!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more wrong?

jokes.text: Your money's mine, Greene. / Your fly's open, Geller.
jokes.setup: Monica and Ross are trash-talking each other during a card game
jokes.punchline: Ross's trash-talk is 'Your fly's open, Geller' — classic misdirection tactic that reveals the game is intensely competitive even within family
jokes.explanation: A quick character moment — the competitive Geller-sibling dynamic is well-established. The trash-talk is funny because of who's doing it. The 'fly' taunt is a classic but not especially inventive.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is not fair! I grew up in this apartment! My whole life is here!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You can't just take it away from me!

jokes.text: You know what I just realized? 'Joker' is 'poker' with a 'J'! / Coincidence? / That's 'joincidence' with a 'C'!
jokes.setup: Joey is at the poker table with Monica and Ross
jokes.punchline: Joey's thunderstruck realization that 'joker' rhymes with/resembles 'poker' (it doesn't, really — but that's the joke), followed by his recursive wordplay error 'joincidence' for 'coincidence'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. Joey's 'discovery' that joker/poker share a letter is a perfect display of his lovable dim-wittedness. But the genius is the second beat: 'That's joincidence with a C' — Joey invents a malapropism to correct his own observation, which is exactly wrong in a way that requires weird backward thinking. This is a carefully constructed joke pretending to be an accidental one. High marks across all dimensions.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It was nice knowing you.

jokes.text: Look! Ugly Naked Guy lit a bunch of candles. / [beat] / That had to hurt!
jokes.setup: The Ugly Naked Guy — a recurring visual gag from across-the-street neighbors — is spotted in the window with candles
jokes.punchline: After a beat of watching, one of them observes 'That had to hurt' — implying something physically disastrous involving the naked man and candles
jokes.explanation: The Ugly Naked Guy is a beloved running gag from earlier seasons. The two-beat structure (lighting candles → reaction) works perfectly. The ellipsis of showing the disaster and replacing it with a reaction line is well-constructed. The implied physical comedy lands.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, he's standing right there!

jokes.text: Rachel, you want to put the marshmallows in concentric circles. / No, Mon. You want to put them in concentric circles. I want to do this. / [does something her own way]
jokes.setup: Monica is directing Rachel on the precise method of placing marshmallows — the kind of overly specific instruction only Monica would give
jokes.punchline: Rachel's correction that Monica WANTS the precision, not Rachel — drawing the boundary between Monica's compulsiveness and everyone else's indifference
jokes.explanation: Very character-specific. The joke is essentially about Monica projecting her compulsive preferences as universal truths. 'No, Mon — YOU want to' is a sharp correction that perfectly captures the Monica-Rachel dynamic. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What were you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm planning to write the same message on Chandler himself.

jokes.text: Every year. [said with resigned exasperation as Monica and Rachel repeat the same marshmallow argument]
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel have the same argument about Thanksgiving food preparation
jokes.punchline: One of the guys delivers 'Every year' as a tired, knowing acknowledgment that this fight is a Thanksgiving tradition
jokes.explanation: Two-word punchline that works on shared history. Economy is its greatest strength — the whole joke lives in the resigned delivery of 'Every year.' Functional and character-appropriate.

jokes.text: It's stuck! / How did it get on? / I put it on to scare Chandler. / Oh, my God! Monica's going to totally freak out! / Plus, it smells really bad in here. / Of course it smells bad. You have your head up a turkey's ass.
jokes.setup: Joey has gotten his head stuck inside a raw turkey
jokes.punchline: Ross's deadpan observation: 'Of course it smells bad. You have your head up a turkey's ass.'
jokes.explanation: A beloved physical comedy set piece. The visual of Joey walking around with a turkey on his head is inherently funny. Ross's matter-of-fact explanation is the best line, delivering the blunt logic that makes the moment complete. The visual element is key — works better on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This has been a great Thanksgiving. You know, usually my holidays are a lot like my apartment before Monica moved in — empty, cold, and filled with a strange smell I can't identify.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! / Who is that? / It's Joey. / I got it! If we win, they have to get rid of the rooster.
jokes.setup: Monica sees Joey with the turkey on his head and doesn't recognize him
jokes.punchline: Monica's horrified reaction, the reveal that it's Joey, and then immediately Chandler pivots to negotiating — 'If we win, they have to get rid of the rooster' — treating a surreal situation as a game-show opportunity
jokes.explanation: The turkey scene continues with good escalation. Chandler's instant pivot to game strategy while Joey has a turkey on his head is delightfully absurd character writing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, wait. You can't move to Westchester. That's like... that's like Connecticut!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not that far.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It might as well be. Look, I'm gonna tell you something. I've ranked all the chesters. Manchester? Great. Winchester? Also great. Westchester? Not great.

jokes.text: If you win, we give up the bird. / But if we win... we get your apartment.
jokes.setup: Joey (turkey-headed) has proposed a deal about the rooster
jokes.punchline: Chandler dramatically raises the stakes — from a pet rooster to the entire apartment — as if this is a reasonable escalation
jokes.explanation: Classic escalation joke that also serves as a plot hinge. The absurdity of using a turkey-head incident as leverage to win an apartment is perfectly absurd. The pause before the reveal of the counter-offer is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm sorry about the house, man.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I really wish the timing had worked out differently. Would've saved me from a lot of awkwardness.

jokes.text: Deal! / What?
jokes.setup: Chandler has proposed getting the apartment if they win the bet
jokes.punchline: Monica instantly accepts without hesitation; Chandler's 'What?' reveals he didn't expect her to agree — he may have been bluffing
jokes.explanation: Brilliant two-word exchange. 'Deal! / What?' tells us everything: Monica's competitive fearlessness, and Chandler's surprised realization that she meant it. Maximum economy for maximum comedy. Monica's compulsive need to win is perfectly captured.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Nancy, thanks for showing us this place.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So... are you single?

jokes.text: Monica's nickname when she was a hockey goalie? / Big Fat Goalie. / Correct!
jokes.setup: In the high-stakes apartment quiz, Ross reads a question about Monica's old hockey nickname
jokes.punchline: 'Big Fat Goalie' — a brutal, specific detail that Monica would never have volunteered but can't deny
jokes.explanation: A great character-specific detail that works because it references Monica's past weight (a recurring character history element) in a maximally undignified nickname. The specificity is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so one of us has to tell everyone about the house.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rock, paper, scissors?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Best two out of three.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Rock, paper, scissors, shoot!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh! I have scissors.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have paper. You win.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? No, you won. Paper covers rock.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I thought you said you had scissors?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I do! Best two out of three!

jokes.text: Rachel claims it's her favorite movie. / Dangerous Liaisons. / Her actual favorite movie is... / Weekend at Bernie's.
jokes.setup: Quiz question distinguishes between Rachel's publicly claimed favorite movie and her real one
jokes.punchline: Rachel's real favorite movie is Weekend at Bernie's — the gap between her cultured self-presentation and her actual taste is the joke
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. The Dangerous Liaisons vs. Weekend at Bernie's dichotomy perfectly encapsulates Rachel's persona gap. The structure (claimed vs. actual) is clean, and the specific choice of Weekend at Bernie's is inspired — lowbrow enough to be embarrassing, beloved enough to be true.

jokes.text: Monica categorizes her towels. How many categories are there? / Everyday use. Fancy. Guest. Fancy guest. / Two seconds. / Eleven? / Unbelievable! Eleven is correct.
jokes.setup: Quiz question asks how many towel categories Monica has
jokes.punchline: The answer is eleven — an absurd number that Monica's friends can't guess, though Monica rattles off four immediately as if that's normal
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's signature jokes. 'Eleven' towel categories is an inspired number — just specific enough to be believable for Monica, just excessive enough to be absurd. Monica spontaneously rattling off 'Everyday use, Fancy, Guest, Fancy guest' in her sleep, then not being able to get to eleven, while Chandler guesses it correctly is a perfect character ensemble moment. High marks across the board.

jokes.text: Chandler was how old when he first touched a girl's breast? / 14? / No, 19. / Thanks, man.
jokes.setup: Quiz question about Chandler's late-blooming experience with women
jokes.punchline: Chandler's correct answer is 19 (old), which Joey guessed as 14 — and Chandler's dry 'Thanks, man' to the expectation of 14 is mortified gratitude
jokes.explanation: Good character joke with a callback to Chandler's established awkward-with-women backstory. 'Thanks, man' is perfectly mortified. The joke is in the gap between expectation and reality, plus Chandler's resigned response.

jokes.text: Joey had an imaginary childhood friend. His name was... / Maurice! / His profession was... / Space cowboy!
jokes.setup: Quiz question about Joey's imaginary childhood friend
jokes.punchline: The imaginary friend's name was 'Maurice' and he was a 'space cowboy' — maximally specific and wonderfully absurd
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best. 'Maurice' and 'space cowboy' are individually funny, but together they're perfect — a strangely formal name paired with an impossible occupation. It's funny because it's so specific (Joey clearly thought hard about this imaginary friend) and so random. Monica's instant, excited recall of 'Space cowboy!' is a great delivery beat. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: What is Chandler Bing's job? / [ten-second silence] / Something to do with transponding. / He's a transponster! / That's not even a word!
jokes.setup: High-stakes quiz question: what is Chandler's job?
jokes.punchline: After ten seconds of silence, they can only say 'something to do with transponding,' then Rachel invents the word 'transponster' — and Monica, losing everything, screams 'That's not even a word!'
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the most iconic Friends moments. 'Transponster' is a perfect piece of comedy writing: it references the ongoing series joke that none of the friends know what Chandler does for a living, escalates through a ten-second pause (perfect timing), and pays off with a made-up word so confidently wrong that Monica loses it. 'That's not even a word!' is a great punchline because it's simultaneously the most and least important problem she has right now. This is 9+ territory — it became a cultural touchstone for the show.

jokes.text: You are mean boys who are just being mean!
jokes.setup: Monica and Rachel have just lost the apartment bet due to the Chandler's-job question
jokes.punchline: Monica's breakdown — 'mean boys who are just being mean' — a perfectly redundant, petulant outburst that reveals her competitive collapse
jokes.explanation: Monica's competitive breakdown delivered with maximum redundancy — 'mean boys who are just being mean' — is funny because the repetition signals emotional collapse. Character-perfect for Monica when losing.

jokes.text: I saw what you were doing in the window! I saw what you're doing to my sister! Get out here!
jokes.setup: Ross storms in furiously — from an earlier season's episode, Ross has seen Chandler kissing Monica through the window
jokes.punchline: Ross's dramatic accusation frames the reveal of Monica and Chandler's relationship — played for maximum dramatic comedy
jokes.explanation: The beginning of the Monica-Chandler reveal scene — an iconic Friends moment. Ross's protective fury is played for laughs through the rapid pivot from accusations to revelations. Strong moment for long-term viewers.

jokes.text: Listen, we had a good run. What was it? Four, five months? That's more than most people have in a lifetime. Goodbye.
jokes.setup: Ross is furiously confronting them from outside; Chandler thinks they're done
jokes.punchline: Chandler's premature resignation speech — eulogizing the relationship before it's even over — delivered with resigned acceptance
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in-character for Chandler — his default mode when threatened is self-sabotage and premature surrender. 'That's more than most people have in a lifetime. Goodbye.' is delivered with appropriate theatrical tragedy. Good character comedy.

jokes.text: Hey, Ross. What's up, bro?
jokes.setup: Ross is furious and Chandler knows why
jokes.punchline: Chandler greets a fuming Ross with casual bro-speak — 'What's up, bro?' — an absurdly deflective non-reaction to being caught with someone's sister
jokes.explanation: Chandler's deployment of casual 'bro' energy in a moment of maximum tension is perfectly on-brand. The deliberate casualness is the joke — it's how Chandler handles confrontation he can't escape.

jokes.text: I think Ross knows about me and Monica. / Dude, he's right there.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are standing right next to a furious Ross
jokes.punchline: Chandler speaks about Ross as if he's not present; Joey's flat correction 'Dude, he's right there' points out the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Joey's grounding 'Dude, he's right there' is a good straight-man moment in a heightened situation. Decent economy.

jokes.text: This is the last box of your clothes. I'm just gonna label it 'What were you thinking?'
jokes.setup: Rachel is helping Monica move in with Chandler (from an older context)
jokes.punchline: Rachel labels the box 'What were you thinking?' — a passive-aggressive editorial comment embedded in a mundane moving task
jokes.explanation: Good dry humor from Rachel — using a moving chore to express her feelings about Monica's choice. Character-appropriate.

jokes.text: I was gonna go across the hall and write that on Chandler.
jokes.setup: Rachel has labeled a box 'What were you thinking?' for Monica
jokes.punchline: Ross reveals he planned to literally write that phrase on Chandler — a comically petty act of sibling revenge
jokes.explanation: Good callback that escalates the previous joke. Ross's plan to write the message ON CHANDLER (as a person) rather than a box is a satisfying absurd escalation.

jokes.text: Guys, I don't wanna make things worse, but I don't want to live with Rachel anymore. You're so mean to each other. I don't wanna end up like that with Rachel. I still like you.
jokes.setup: In the midst of emotional chaos, Phoebe interjects with her own concern
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's statement 'I don't wanna make things worse, but...' followed by something that makes things significantly worse — delivered with earnest concern about not wanting to end up 'like that' with Rachel, to Rachel's face
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she is simultaneously empathetic and completely tone-deaf. 'I still like you' said to Rachel while rejecting living with her is a funny, sincere-offensive line.

jokes.text: Phoebe, you gotta take her. / I said some bad stuff, but Rachel has qualities that make her a good roommate. She gets tons of catalogs and folds down the pages of things I'd like.
jokes.setup: Phoebe doesn't want Rachel as a roommate; Monica is trying to sell Rachel's good qualities
jokes.punchline: Monica's list of Rachel's virtues begins with 'she folds down catalog pages to things I'd like' — a bizarrely specific and self-serving 'compliment' about Rachel's service to Monica
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy — Monica's 'defense' of Rachel reveals how transactional and Monica-centric the relationship has been. The catalog detail is specific and funny.

jokes.text: When I take a shower, she leaves me notes on the mirror. / I do. I do do that. / That's nice. I like having things to read in the bathroom.
jokes.setup: Monica continues listing Rachel's virtues for Phoebe
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's completely sincere 'I like having things to read in the bathroom' — treating a sweet roommate gesture as primarily a reading-material issue
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's reframing of a sweet gesture as bathroom reading material is a funny minor beat. 'I do do that' from Rachel (self-conscious affirmation) also adds to the gentle comedy.

jokes.text: When I fall asleep on the couch, she covers me with a blanket. / Well, you know, I don't want you to be cold.
jokes.setup: Monica is making the case for Rachel as roommate by listing small kindnesses
jokes.punchline: Rachel's explanation of why she covers Monica with a blanket — 'I don't want you to be cold' — is so earnest and simple that it cuts through the comedic premise and becomes a genuinely sweet moment, which is itself the joke
jokes.explanation: More of a sweet moment than a hard joke, but Friends often plays this register. The humor is light — Rachel's earnestness against the comedic context.

jokes.text: And now you have to leave. And I have to live with a boy!
jokes.setup: Monica has been emotionally recounting all of Rachel's sweet qualities, building to genuine sentimentality
jokes.punchline: The pivot: Monica snaps out of sentiment to complain 'I have to live with a boy!' — referring to Chandler, her fiancé/husband, with minor horror
jokes.explanation: The pivot from genuine sentiment to 'I have to live with a boy!' is perfectly timed. The word 'boy' (instead of 'man' or 'Chandler') adds the right register of childlike horror. Good economy and character-specific to Monica's control issues.

jokes.text: Can I ask you a question? / Sure. / What the hell is that dog doing here?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey have a new roommate situation; Chandler notices something unexpected
jokes.punchline: Chandler's formal setup ('Can I ask you a question?') followed by the flat absurdity of 'What the hell is that dog doing here?'
jokes.explanation: Joey's unexplained dog is a nice absurdist detail. The formal preamble ('Can I ask you a question?') before the exasperated payoff is good structural comedy. Visual element (the dog) enhances it.

jokes.text: I think because it didn't involve divorce... or projectile vomiting.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is toasting a Thanksgiving that turned out better than expected
jokes.punchline: Her bar for a successful holiday is 'no divorce and no projectile vomiting' — an absurdly low benchmark delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Funny because 'projectile vomiting' is so specific — Phoebe clearly has a past Thanksgiving trauma. The combination of 'divorce' (emotional) and 'projectile vomiting' (physical) as the two categories of Thanksgiving failure is nicely absurd.

jokes.text: ...syphilis and stuff... we wouldn't be all together. So I guess what I'm trying to say is that I'm very thankful that all of your Thanksgivings sucked.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is building a toast about how circumstances brought them together
jokes.punchline: 'I'm very thankful that all of your Thanksgivings sucked' — a perfectly inverted Thanksgiving toast that expresses genuine love through brutal honesty about being glad others suffered
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's warmer laughs. The 'syphilis and stuff' as a throwaway is characteristically Phoebe-absurd. But 'I'm thankful that all your Thanksgivings sucked' is a genuinely clever inversion of Thanksgiving sentiment — it's loving and terrible at the same time. Structurally sound with good payoff.

jokes.text: Here's to a lousy Christmas! / And a crappy New Year!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just toasted to everyone's Thanksgivings sucking
jokes.punchline: The group extends the logic to future holidays — toasting to lousy Christmases and crappy New Years — embracing the inverted sentiment
jokes.explanation: A quick, satisfying callback that extends the joke's logic. 'Crappy New Year' has good rhythm. The group joining in gives it communal energy.

jokes.text: You can't move. You just-- You just can't. / Rachel's right. This is where you guys belong. You don't wanna live in Westchester. That's the worst of the Chesters.
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to argue against Chandler and Monica moving to Westchester
jokes.punchline: 'That's the worst of the Chesters' — Joey produces a confident comparative ranking of Chesters (Manchester, Rochester, Winchester, etc.) that he clearly has no basis for, delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Joey jokes. The authority with which Joey ranks the Chesters — with zero actual knowledge — is the perfect expression of his character. 'That's the worst of the Chesters' implies he's carefully evaluated all the Chesters and reached this conclusion. Highly quotable and pure character comedy.

jokes.text: Sometimes when I'm alone in my apartment, I look over here and you guys are just having dinner or watching TV or something, but it makes me feel better.
jokes.setup: Ross is making a sentimental speech about why Chandler and Monica shouldn't move
jokes.punchline: Ross's admission that he watches his friends through the window when he's lonely is simultaneously touching and mildly creepy — the comedy is in what he doesn't realize he's confessing
jokes.explanation: A bittersweet-funny moment. The inadvertent creepiness of Ross's window-watching confession gives an otherwise tender speech an unexpected comic dimension.

jokes.text: And now when I look over, who am I gonna see? The Gottliebs? The Yangs? They don't make me feel so good.
jokes.setup: Ross continues his speech about how much he depends on seeing his friends through the window
jokes.punchline: His substitution of neighbor names 'The Gottliebs' and 'The Yangs' — implying he already knows his alternative window-watching subjects — adds absurd specificity to his loneliness
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the previous joke. The names 'Gottliebs' and 'Yangs' make Ross's window-stalking both more specific and more absurd. The delivery of 'They don't make me feel so good' adds a nice sad-funny quality.

jokes.text: So don't move, okay? Just stay here, and maybe close your blinds at night.
jokes.setup: Ross has been making an emotional speech about watching his friends through the window
jokes.punchline: His final request — 'and maybe close your blinds at night' — is an accidental acknowledgment that he's been watching them at inappropriate hours, undercutting his entire heartfelt speech
jokes.explanation: The punchline that cashes in the entire window-watching bit. The genius is that Ross adds 'close your blinds at night' as a postscript, which retroactively makes everything he said funnier — he wasn't just occasionally glancing over, he was watching at night. Structurally excellent callback payoff.

jokes.text: Yeah, and about this Nancy... If you're not sleeping with her, should I?
jokes.setup: Everyone is wrapping up — Chandler's affair accusation is fully resolved, Nancy confirmed as just a realtor
jokes.punchline: Joey's pragmatic pivot: since Chandler isn't sleeping with the attractive realtor, could he?
jokes.explanation: Joey's opportunistic logic is very on-brand — once an attractive woman is confirmed available, he moves. The callback to the affair plot is clean and the economy is sharp.

jokes.text: What? / We got the house. / Oh, my God. / I didn't wanna tell you in front of them. / We got it?! We got the house?! We're getting a house!
jokes.setup: Monica is told by Chandler that the house offer was rejected — everyone leaves, apologizing
jokes.punchline: The 'rejection' was a lie — Chandler didn't want to tell them in front of the friends. The reveal that they GOT the house is played as a comedic twist after the emotional false ending
jokes.explanation: A plot-level misdirection played for comedy. Chandler's quiet lie to protect the moment is sweet and funny. Monica's escalating excitement ('We got it?! We got the house?!') is a great reaction.

jokes.text: We're getting a house. / And a baby. / We're growing up. / We sure are. / Who's gonna tell them? / Not it! / Not it! Damn it!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica celebrate getting the house — a big life milestone
jokes.punchline: The celebration is immediately followed by playing 'Not it!' to avoid being the one who has to tell their friends — reverting to childlike behavior immediately after declaring 'we're growing up'
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant joke that earns its score. The juxtaposition is perfect: 'We're growing up' immediately contradicted by 'Not it!' — playing a children's avoidance game. The structure creates the joke, and 'Damn it!' from the loser is a satisfying payoff. High marks for economy and structure.

jokes.text: Rachel, this is yours. / Why? What are these for? / You'll see. / All right, everybody open them. / Wow, this is so beautiful! / These are the ones I was looking at in the store! / I know. / Oh, I love this! / A meatball sub! / Thanks! / Seriously, guys, what's going on? What are these for? / Well, I didn't know how to tell you before, but we got the house. / Enjoy!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler hand out personalized gifts — jewelry to the women, apparently — building to a reveal
jokes.punchline: Joey's gift is a meatball sub; everyone else's are beautiful jewelry/personal items. Joey's delighted 'Thanks!' followed by his genuine bafflement about what 'these' could be for (while holding a sandwich) is perfect
jokes.explanation: A great closing joke. Monica and Chandler personalize their goodbye gifts — everyone gets meaningful jewelry, Joey gets a meatball sub. The fact that Joey is thrilled ('Thanks!') and then baffled about what the gifts 'mean' (he's holding a sandwich) is perfect character comedy. 'Enjoy!' as the reveal of the news is a nice button.

tmdb_overview: After Phoebe and Rachel catch Chandler getting into a car with an unknown blonde woman, they follow them to the suburbs. Fearing that Chandler is cheating on Monica, they inform her and learn that the woman is a real estate agent. The pair has been secretly shopping for houses and struggling with how to tell their best friends about their plans. Together the friends reminisce about their good times in the apartment.
insight: Fifty jokes in 19 minutes, but weak landing undermines final-season momentum.
